accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are accurate and qualified. Teaching-only reserved hierarchy, ordinary TTL versus serve-stale, negative versus failure caching and DNSSEC versus HTTPS prevent common false cutover/security guarantees.

evidence.quote: Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

mechanisms.reason: Resolver actors/referrals and alias chase establish where cached state lives. Timed address example, negative lifetime, failover reuse and diagnostic stages explain cause/effect; both diagrams preserve actor and cache ownership.

evidence.quote: A resolver caches the old address at 10:00 with a 300-second TTL. At 10:01 we change the address and lower TTL to 30 seconds. Its existing entry can still be ordinarily usable until 10:05; the edit does not rewrite that entry.

coherence.reason: Discovery precedes authorities and record types, then cache changes/absence, steering, diagnosis and trust. All eight card criteria groups build on defined state and actors; actual learner transfers follow these mechanisms.

evidence.quote: The recursive resolver returns the result to the stub. Cached answers can avoid authority visits, and cached delegations can let it start closer to the answer. The stub need not perform each visit itself.

decisions.reason: Provides advance TTL reduction, monitored overlap, short-TTL cost, healthy replacement headroom, resolver-first diagnosis and mandatory HTTPS identity checks. Redundancy and DNSSEC are limited to their actual responsibilities.

evidence.quote: Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing. An authoritative new address beside a cached old one suggests a cache-age question, not an automatic need for another edit.

clarity.reason: Defines name, address, record, cache, stub, resolver, zone, delegation, alias, TTL and negative statuses before applying them. Concrete times and distinct error cases carry useful explanation. Every learner quote is exact and supports the associated reasoning.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.

outcomes.reason: All eight criteria met: stub delegates lookup to recursive resolver, which follows referrals to authoritative zone data. A/AAAA supply address families; CNAME requires target address data and independently cacheable records. Cached answers/delegations skip visits; hostname resolution precedes separate HTTPS/path exchange and proves no application health.

All three criteria met: 11:59 plus 3600 seconds permits ordinary use until 12:59; new TTL does not rewrite old state. Lower early, age prior TTL, overlap and monitor both endpoints/connections. Extra queries/dependency and stale-serving/open-connection caveats prevent a universal cutoff; no unsupported shutdown duration invented.

All three criteria: negative absence result has its own remaining lifetime, not new positive TTL. NXDOMAIN differs from existing-name missing AAAA; SERVFAIL says failure to resolve, not absence, and can be cached. Exact remaining negative lifetime correctly left unspecified.

All four criteria: separate detection/policy changes answers, shared caches and multiple requests per connection invalidate exact HTTP split, stale address/open connections prevent instant move, and west requires reachable healthy spare capacity.

All four criteria: cache/open connection explains continuing users while fresh resolution fails; inspect client resolver name/type/status/TTL then authority/delegation. Expected address followed by HTTP500 is a distinct service error; alternate DNS servers cannot fix shared bad data or failed Notes.

All three criteria: signatures and configured trust-chain validate DNS origin/integrity, not query secrecy, app health or availability. HTTPS still checks requested api.notes.example identity, including alias case, and encrypts HTTP.

sourceChecks.claim: Cloudflare verifies name/address discovery, resolver cache and HTTP exchange after lookup. Lesson correctly restricts DNS to hostname rather than copying the source page casual URL wording. Application health is a separate observation.

AWS verifies root/TLD/domain resolver traversal and cached delegation shortcuts. RFC1034 section5.3.1 verifies local stub/recursive distinction. Supplement https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2606.html confirms reserved teaching names; diagram explicitly labels a hypothetical hierarchy, not public .test delegation.

AWS verifies A IPv4, AAAA IPv6 and CNAME name target. RFC1034 section3.6.2 verifies following aliases, optionally returning target data together and caching CNAME separately. No address exists merely from alias text.

RFC8767 verifies ordinary TTL duration and permitted stale data after failed refresh. RFC1034 section3.6.1 supports reducing TTL before planned change. Existing TTL arithmetic and no cache-push/connection migration are correct; diagram accurately shows old 300-second state against new 30-second authority.

RFC9520 distinguishes useful absence answers from resolution failure and requires failure caching in conforming resolvers. Supplement https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2308.html sections3–5 verifies negative TTL from SOA and separate name/type caching. New positive TTL cannot reset the existing negative entry.

AWS verifies health checks and policy as explicit mechanisms for DNS failover. Shared-cache behavior from RFC1034 and separate HTTP exchange explain non-proportional request traffic and no connection migration. Replacement capacity and sampled health are necessary conditions, not supplied by DNS.

RFC1034 verifies resolver caches, delegation traversal, alternative servers and failure results. Supplement https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html defines HTTP500 as server response failure. Diagnostic sequence correctly separates resolution from TLS/HTTP and limits what redundant DNS repairs.

RFC4033 verifies configured trust anchors, signature chain, data integrity/origin, unsigned-data limits, no confidentiality or DoS protection. Supplement https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9525.html section6.1.2 gives HTTPS reference identity from URL hostname. Alias lookup does not remove certificate validation; application authorization remains separate.
